blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: An inherited warehouse model's LP solution has every 'warehouse open' binary between 0.3 and 0.6, while nearly all of its 2,000 assignment binaries are 0 or 1. Where should the audit look first?

options.text: At the objective's costs on the open switches and the assignments
options.says: The costs decide which point is best, but the rows decide which fractional points are allowed; the page traced the fractions to the rows that hold the switches.

options.text: At the rows linking assignments to the open switches they need
options.says: Right: fractional switches with whole assignments are the signature of a weak linking row, as the twelve fronts at 0.38 to 0.64 were.

options.text: At the assignment rows, since the 2,000 assignments are most of the model
options.says: Those variables are whole already; the fractional ones are the switches, and they point at the rows that hold them.

options.text: At the solver settings for the open binaries, since an LP should return whole numbers
options.says: An LP relaxation returns fractions whenever the rows allow them; no setting changes that, a stronger row does.

origin.section: The LP Point Shows Where a Formulation Is Weak

questions.stem: After a reformulation, a model's LP bound falls by 16%, HiGHS's bound after its root node is unchanged, and the solve to the production gap takes twice as many nodes. What should the team report?

options.text: A faster model, since its LP bound is 16% tighter
options.says: The page measured the opposite on GridCap medium: equal root bounds, then 7,823 nodes against 3,856.

options.text: A broken model, since the root bound did not move
options.says: The new rows change the formulation's own LP bound; equal root bounds only show that the solver's presolve and cuts made up the difference.

options.text: A measurement to repeat, since node counts vary between runs
options.says: HiGHS's node counts repeat on the same model; the module's tests run a solve twice and check it.

options.text: A tighter LP bound, with no speed-up for this solver on this data
options.says: Right: that is the case study's own verdict, keeping the strong form for its bound and not claiming a speed-up.

origin.section: The Solver's Own Work Decides Whether a Reformulation Solves Faster

questions.stem: On a portfolio whose yearly budgets are about 20 times its largest yearly project spend, the audit finds no start to fix and no new conflict from the budget rows. Why?

options.text: Presolve had already removed every start that could be fixed
options.says: The audit reads the model as built, before any solver runs; nothing was removed from it.

options.text: Conflicts only ever come from two starts of the same project
options.says: Capacity rows give conflicts too: on GridCap small with crew rows they gave 70 new ones.

options.text: No single start, nor any pair, can overflow a year's room
options.says: Right: fixings and conflicts need starts that are large next to what a row leaves; here even two together use a tenth of it.

options.text: Budget rows are equalities, so they can never fix a start
options.says: The budget rows are inequalities (spend at most the budget), and on tiny and small such rows did fix starts.
